props.title: She's All That
props.initialSlug: Popular jock bets he can transform school outcast

sections.content: She's All That perfectly captures the late 90s teen movie renaissance, following Clueless (1995) and setting the template for countless makeover rom-coms. The film cleverly modernizes George Bernard Shaw's Pygmalion with high school social dynamics, starring Freddie Prinze Jr. as popular jock Zack who bets he can transform "nerdy" art student Laney (Rachael Leigh Cook) into prom queen. While the premise might seem problematic today, the film's charm lies in how it subverts expectations - Laney's "transformation" is mostly superficial, and Zack is the one who truly changes by learning to see past social hierarchies.

sections.content: The film emerged during a golden age of teen cinema, alongside 10 Things I Hate About You (1999) and Drive Me Crazy (1999). These films shared DNA with John Hughes' earlier works like Pretty in Pink (1986), but added self-aware humor and contemporary soundtracks. She's All That particularly excels in its supporting cast, including Paul Walker, Anna Paquin, and a scene-stealing Matthew Lillard, whose infamous dance sequence to "Rock Your Body" became an iconic moment of 90s pop culture.

The makeover trope reached peak saturation after She's All That, spawning direct responses like Not Another Teen Movie (2001) and gender-flipped versions like The New Guy (2002). Yet the film's influence extends beyond parody - its DNA is evident in modern teen films like To All the Boys I've Loved Before (2018) and The DUFF (2015), which similarly explore social transformation while attempting to subvert traditional beauty standards. sections.content: While She's All That followed familiar beats of 90s teen romance, it marked a transition point between classical teen movies and more socially conscious modern takes. Compare its handling of class and social status to later films like A Cinderella Story (2004) or Easy A (2010), which more directly challenge systemic social hierarchies. The film's legacy is complicated - both a product of its time and a stepping stone toward more nuanced teen storytelling.
